 CHIEF JUSTICE ROBERTS:  We'll hear

 Mr. McNamara.
 ORAL ARGUMENT OF ROBERT J. McNAMARA
 ON BEHALF OF THE PETITIONERS
 MR. McNAMARA: Mr. Chief Justice, and
may it please the Court:
 The Natural Gas Act authorizes private
companies to ask courts to order the forced
 sale of private property, but it says nothing
 about the substantive law those courts should
use to determine what that property is worth.
 That silence matters because, on its own,
 authorizing companies to file condemnations
does nothing to preempt state laws defining the
 measure of compensation.
 As this Court held in Jones and as
Congress and the courts would have known in
1947, the right of eminent domain is just the
 power to take property.  It's separate from an
individual's right to just compensation, which
 flows from a different source.

North Dakota law provides that source
 here. On its face, it imposes even-handed
 obligations on anyone who condemns land in that
 state, including WBI. The Fifth Amendment
places a floor on that compensation but not a
 ceiling.
 Now, to be sure, North Dakota law
 wouldn't apply to the United States if it took
 land in its own name, but that's not because of
 some special trait of the federal eminent
 domain cause of action.  It's because the
 United States is sovereign.  And private
 companies aren't sovereign.  They're private
 delegees.  And this Court has consistently said
 that distinction matters.
 Nothing in the statute extends the
United States' sovereign immunity to private
 companies, and that means they don't have it.
That's what Congress would have expected in
 1947, which was just three years after this
 Court in Davies Warehouse reaffirmed its
longstanding custom of looking to state law to
give meaning and content to federal statutes.
 Silence meant state law then.  Silence means
 state law today.
